comparator.sourceNotes: The current official programme page defines three years of eight courses per year. Year 1 contains six compulsory 7.5-EC foundation courses and two 7.5-EC choices. Year 2 contains four compulsory 7.5-EC courses and four 7.5-EC choices. The shared official 2026-27 Physics major document identifies the same compulsory foundation course codes and confirms that NS-310B Bachelor Research is a compulsory 15-EC advanced component; the remaining 45 EC of Year 3 is elective. The current official CursusPlanner lists the programme's physics electives as 7.5-EC courses across levels 1-3. Genuine year-specific elective space is preserved as such rather than filled with an invented specialization. These components account for exactly 180 EC.
components: Compulsory Year-1 experimental and analytical training.
Compulsory Year-1 astronomy and optics foundation.
Two genuine 7.5-EC choices from the published Year-1 physics elective offer; subjects are not invented.
Four genuine 7.5-EC choices from the published Year-2 physics elective offer; subjects are not invented.
Compulsory advanced physics research and bachelor-thesis component.
Six genuine 7.5-EC choices from the published advanced physics elective offer; subjects are not invented.

exception.reason: Utrecht's 180-EC Physics and Astronomy bachelor is defined by compulsory relativistic and classical mechanics, electromagnetism, astronomy and optics, quantum mechanics, statistical physics, three successive mathematical-techniques courses, experimental data acquisition, an experimental research project, advanced physics electives and a 15-EC physics research thesis. UCR offers useful supporting study in mathematics, programming, data science, Earth systems, climate and energy, but no course whose disciplinary object is physics or astronomy and no mechanics, electromagnetism, optics, quantum physics, statistical physics, thermodynamics or experimental-physics laboratory sequence. A 24-course UCR response would therefore be a mathematics/data/Earth-science programme adjacent to some physics applications, not a defensible Physics and Astronomy curriculum.
exception.curriculumContext: The current curriculum accounts for exactly 180 EC: Year 1 comprises six compulsory 7.5-EC foundations and 15 EC of physics choices; Year 2 comprises Quantum Mechanics, Statistical Physics, Mathematical Techniques 3 and Experimental Research Project plus 30 EC of physics choices; Year 3 comprises the compulsory 15-EC Bachelor Research/Thesis and 45 EC of advanced physics choices. The programme's published elective offer spans climate physics, experimental physics, theoretical physics, astronomy, quantum matter, field theory, subatomic physics, cosmology, fluid mechanics and biological/soft-matter physics. No formal route is imposed, so the genuine elective spaces remain unfilled rather than being assigned an invented specialization.
exception.ucrCourseEvidence: Reviewed all 151 current enriched UCR course rows, including names, descriptions, outline-derived profiles, disciplines, topics, methods, prerequisites and planned semesters. DISGATE102 Mathematical Methods, DISMATH211 Linear Algebra, DISMATH214 Advanced Calculus, DISMATH213 Computational & Numerical Methods, DISMATH312 Linear Systems and DISMATH314 Probability & Statistics provide substantial mathematical preparation. DISGATE101 Introduction to Programming, DISDATA111 Introduction to Data Science and related computing courses can support numerical work. ENSENVI111 Dynamic Earth, ENSENVI213 Earth System Science Tools, ENSSUST111 Climate Change, ENSSUST211 Energy & Sustainability and ENSSUST311 Renewable System Design address Earth, climate and energy applications. None is a physics or astronomy course. The workbook contains no classical or relativistic mechanics, electromagnetism, optics, quantum mechanics, statistical physics, thermodynamics, astrophysics, particle physics, condensed-matter physics, physics laboratory, experimental-physics research project or physics thesis sequence. Life Science Laboratory is specifically biological rather than physical. Filling 23 non-PPD places would therefore require extensive adjacent mathematics, computing, environmental science and engineering courses that cannot reproduce the programme's defining disciplinary core.
